summary: Defines a Robust Header Compression profile for IP/UDP/RTP packets that uses features of the lower layers to remove the header entirely for most packets in the best case. It extends the ROHC RTP profile. It is standards-track and obsoletes RFC 3242.

plainLanguage.summary: ROHC is a way of shrinking the repetitive headers of real-time packets. This document defines a profile of it that goes one step further than the usual one-byte header: most packets carry no header at all, only their data. That only works if the network layer underneath promises to deliver packets in order and to report every loss, so the missing header can be reconstructed on arrival.

questions: what is a no header packet in rohc
what is a rohc context check packet
subtitle: A header compression profile that removes the compressed header from most packets entirely, by borrowing help from the link below.

tldr.problem: On radio links that are built around one fixed packet size, even a single extra byte of header is expensive, because the packet no longer fits the link's preferred size. The smallest ROHC RTP header is one byte, and that one byte is still too much.
tldr.mechanism: The profile lets the layer below the compressor take over the job of the one-byte header: it identifies packet types, guarantees in-order delivery and reports packet loss, so the sequence number and the check value can be inferred instead of sent.
tldr.outcome: In the best case a packet becomes nothing but its payload. The price is a set of demanding requirements on the assisting layer, so the profile is meant for particular applications over particular links.

today: RFC 4362 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, so it remains the current link-layer assisted ROHC RTP profile. It replaced RFC 3242, and it was later updated by RFC 4815.

sections.title: Why the Header Could Be Removed Entirely
sections.content:
Header compression is a technique used to compress and transparently decompress the header information of a packet on a per-hop basis, utilizing redundancy within individual packets and between consecutive packets within a packet stream. Several protocols have been developed to compress the network and transport protocol headers, and these schemes have been successful in improving efficiency over many wired bottleneck links. In addition, an additional compression scheme called Compressed RTP has been developed to improve compression efficiency further for real-time traffic using RTP.

The schemes mentioned above have all been designed by taking into account normal assumptions about link characteristics, which traditionally have been based on wired links only. With an increasing number of wireless links in the Internet paths, these assumptions are no longer generally valid. In wireless environments, especially wide-coverage cellular environments, relatively high error rates are tolerated in order to allow efficient usage of the radio resources. For real-time traffic, which is more sensitive to delays than to errors, such operating conditions will be normal, for example over third generation cellular links, and header compression must therefore tolerate packet loss.

ROHC RTP has become a very efficient, robust and capable compression scheme, able to compress the headers down to a total size of one octet only. However, other air interfaces will also be used in all-IP networks, with further implications for the header compression issue. These older air interfaces are less flexible, with radio bearers optimized for specific payload sizes. This means that not even a single octet of header can be added without using the next higher fixed packet size supported by the link, which is obviously very costly.

The purpose of the profile is therefore to provide a header-free packet format that, for a certain application behavior, can replace a majority of the one-octet header ROHC RTP packets during normal operation, while still being fully transparent. For other applications, compression is carried out as with normal ROHC RTP. The additional complexity implies that it should only be used to optimize performance of specific applications over specific links.
sections.plainLanguage: Some radio links bill by the packet: a packet of the wrong size wastes airtime. A header of one byte can be the difference between fitting the link's preferred size and having to round up to the next one. So the goal here is to send no header at all, and get the information it would have carried from somewhere else.

sections.title: How the Profile Fits Together
sections.content:
The ROHC IP/UDP/RTP profile defined in the earlier document and updated by this one, profile 0x0005 in hex, is designed to be used over channels that have been optimized for specific payload sizes and that therefore cannot efficiently accommodate header information when transmitted together with payloads corresponding to these optimal sizes.

The LLA profile extends, and thus also inherits all functionality from, the ROHC RTP profile by defining some additional functionality and an interface from the ROHC component towards an assisting lower layer. By imposing additional requirements on the lower layers compared to the ROHC framework, it is possible to infer the information needed to maintain robust and transparent header compression, even though the headers are completely eliminated during most of the operation time. Basically, this profile replaces the smallest and most frequent ROHC headers with a no-header format, for which the header functionality must be provided by other means.

The fields present in the ROHC RTP headers for U/O-mode packet type 0 are the packet type identifier, the sequence number and the CRC. The subsequent sections elaborate on how the functionality of these fields is replaced for the no-header packet.
sections.plainLanguage: The profile is an addition on top of the ordinary ROHC RTP profile, not a replacement. It borrows three jobs from the layer underneath: saying what kind of packet this is, keeping packets in order, and reporting losses. Everything else stays as it was.

sections.title: Replacing the Packet Type, Sequence Number and CRC
sections.content:
All ROHC headers carry a packet type identifier, indicating to the decompressor how the header should be interpreted. This is a function that must be provided by some means in zero-byte header compression. It will be possible to distinguish ROHC RTP packets with compressed headers thanks to the packet type identifier, but a mechanism is needed to separate packets with a header from packets without a header. This function MUST therefore be provided by the assisting layer in one way or another.

From the sending application, the RTP sequence number is increased by one for each packet sent. The purpose of the sequence number is to cope with packet reordering and packet loss. If reordering or loss has occurred before the transmission point, the compressing side can easily avoid problems by not allowing the use of a header-free packet. However, at the transmission point, loss or reordering over the link cannot be anticipated. Therefore, for the no-header packet, the assisting layer MUST guarantee in-order delivery over the link, and at the receiving side it MUST provide an indication for each packet loss over the link. This is basically the same principle that the Van Jacobson header compression relies on.

All context-updating RRP packets carry a CRC calculated over the uncompressed header, used by the decompressor to verify that the updated context is correct. This verification serves three purposes: detection of longer losses than can be covered by the sequence number least significant bits, protection against failures caused by residual bit errors in compressed headers, and protection against faulty implementations and other causes of error. Since this profile defines a no-header packet without this CRC, care must be taken to fulfill these purposes by other means. Detection of long losses is already covered, since the assisting layer must provide an indication of all packet losses. Furthermore, the no-header packet has one important advantage over RHP packets in that residual bit errors cannot damage a header that is not even sent.
sections.plainLanguage: The one-byte header did three things: it said what the packet was, it carried the sequence number, and it carried a checksum. Here the link below takes over the first two, and the third becomes largely unnecessary, because a packet with no header cannot be corrupted in its header.

sections.title: The Three New Packet Types
sections.content:
The LLA profile defines three new packet types to be used in addition to the RRP packet types defined by the ROHC framework.

A No-Header Packet is a packet that consists only of the payload of the original packet. It MAY be used when only the sequence information needs to be conveyed to the decompressor, in other words when all header fields are either unchanged or follow the currently established change pattern. An LLA compressor is not allowed to deliver no-header packets when operating in R-mode. The assisting layer MAY send the no-header packet for a given sequence number only if a no-header packet was delivered by the LLA compressor and the assisting layer can guarantee that the decompressor will infer the proper sequencing, based on the confidence that the decompressor has the means to infer proper sequencing for the preceding packet and has either received a loss indication or the packet itself for it. No-header packets update the context, in that they carry the RTP sequence number.

A Context Synchronization Packet handles the case where the packet stream overruns the channel bandwidth and data is discarded, which may result in decompressor context invalidation. It carries the compressed header without padding and discards the payload, and additionally carries the RTP payload length in two octets, stored in network byte order. This is needed because the decompressor uses the payload length to infer certain fields in the uncompressed header, namely the IPv4 total length, the IPv6 payload length, the UDP length and the IPv4 header checksum field. When the decompressor has received and processed a context synchronization packet, the packet MUST be discarded.

A Context Check Packet carries no payload and only an optional CRC value in addition to the packet type identifier. Its purpose is to provide a useful packet that MAY be sent by a synchronized physical link layer in the case where data must be sent at fixed intervals, even if no compressed packet is available. The C bit indicates whether the CRC field is used. Context check packets do not update context. The decompressor is REQUIRED to handle a context check packet received with the C bit set and to perform context verification, applying the received CRC to the last decompressed packet unless a packet loss indication was previously received. A context check packet received with C=0 MUST be ignored by the decompressor.
sections.plainLanguage: Three new kinds of packet. One is pure payload. One keeps the compressed header but throws the data away, to resynchronise cheaply. One carries nothing but a checksum, so the receiver can confirm it is still in step.

sections.title: The Interface With the Assisting Layer
sections.content:
This profile relies on the lower layers to provide the necessary functionality to allow no-header packets to be sent. The interaction between the LLA compressor and decompressor and the applicable link technology is defined as two interfaces. While the document defines semantics, it does not specify how these interfaces are to be implemented.

The compressor-to-assisting-layer interface defines the following parameters: RRP, RRP segmentation flag, CSP, CSP segmentation flag, no-header packet, and RTP sequence number. All parameters, except the no-header packet, MUST always be delivered to the assisting layer. This leads to two possible delivery scenarios. Either RRP, CSP, CCP, the no-header packet and the RTP sequence number are delivered with the corresponding segmentation flags set, which corresponds to the case when the compressor allows sending of a no-header packet, with or without segmentation applied to the corresponding RRP and CSP packets. Or RRP, CSP, CCP and the RTP sequence number are delivered, which corresponds to the case when the compressor does not allow sending of a no-header packet.

The RTP sequence number MUST be delivered for each packet by the compressor, to allow the assisting layer to maintain the necessary sequencing information.

The assisting-layer-to-decompressor interface defines simple rules for the delivery of received packets. The decompressor needs a way to distinguish no-header packets from packets with a header, and a way to infer the sequencing information. To achieve this, the decompressor MUST receive an indication for each packet loss over the link for CID=0, and the received packet together with an indication of whether the packet received is a no-header packet. The context is updated from a packet loss indication.
sections.plainLanguage: Two conversations happen below the compressor. The compressor tells the link what it produced, including the sequence number of every packet. The link tells the decompressor what arrived, and says explicitly when something was lost. The decompressor cannot work without both.

sections.title: The Optimistic Approach Agreement
sections.content:
ROHC defines an optimistic approach for updates to reduce the header overhead, fully exploited in the Optimistic and Unidirectional modes of operation. Due to the presence of a CRC in all compressed headers, the optimistic approach is defined as a compressor issue only, because the decompressor will always be able to detect an invalid context through the CRC verification.

However, no CRC is present in the no-header packet defined by the LLA profile. Therefore, the loss of an RHP packet updating the context may not always be detected. To avoid this problem, the compressing and decompressing sides must agree on the principles for the optimistic approach, and the agreed principles MUST be enforced not only by the compressor but also by the transmitting assisting layer. If, for example, three consecutive updates are sent to convey a header field change, the decompressor must know this and invalidate the context if three or more consecutive physical packets are lost.

An LLA decompressor MUST use the optimistic approach knowledge to detect possible context loss events. If context loss is suspected, it MUST invalidate the context and not forward any packets before the context has been synchronized. It is REQUIRED that all documents describing how the LLA profile is implemented over a certain link technology define how the optimistic approach is agreed to between the compressing side and the decompressing side. It could be handled with a fixed principle, with negotiation at startup, or by other means, but the method must be unambiguously defined.
sections.plainLanguage: The usual scheme relies on a checksum to notice when the receiver has lost track. Without a checksum, the two ends have to agree in advance, for example, that three lost packets in a row mean a resynchronisation. The rule has to be written down in the document for that particular kind of link.

sections.title: When the Profile Applies
sections.content:
The LLA profile can be used with any link technology capable of providing the required functionality described in the previous sections. Thus, whether LLA or ROHC RTP should be implemented depends on the characteristics of the link itself. For most RTP packet streams, LLA will work exactly as ROHC RTP, and it will have a higher compression efficiency for packet streams with certain characteristics. LLA will never have a lower compression efficiency than ROHC RTP.

LLA, like all other ROHC profiles, is fully transparent to any packet stream reaching the compressor. It does not make any assumptions about the packet stream but will perform optimally for packet streams with certain characteristics, for example synchronized streams exactly timed with the assisting link over which the profile is implemented.

The LLA profile is obviously not applicable if the UDP checksum, which is 2 bytes, is enabled, which is always the case for IPv6/UDP. For IPv4/UDP, the sender may choose to disable the UDP checksum.
sections.plainLanguage: The profile never makes things worse, so it is safe to turn on generally, but it only pays off on links that need it. One hard limit: if the UDP checksum is on, the two bytes it costs more than the header this profile saves, so it cannot be used at all over IPv6.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security considerations of ROHC RTP apply also to this document, with one addition: in the case of a denial-of-service attack scenario where an intruder injects bogus CCP packets using random CRC values onto the link, the CRC check will fail for incorrect reasons at the decompressor side. This would obviously greatly reduce the advantages of ROHC and any extra efficiency provided by this profile due to unnecessary context invalidation, feedback messages and refresh packets. However, the same remarks related to the presence of such an intruder apply.
sections.plainLanguage: The one new risk is that someone on the link can send fake checksum packets and make the receiver throw away its state and start again. That costs performance rather than correctness, and the same objection applies to the intrusion itself.

viz.caption: WHERE THE PROFILE SITS AND WHAT IT RELIES ON

layers.label: ROHC RTP header
layers.detail: One octet carrying the packet type, the sequence number and the CRC

layers.label: LLA profile
layers.detail: Replaces that one octet with a no-header format

layers.label: Assisting layer
layers.detail: Provides packet type identification, ordering and loss indication

layers.label: Link technology
layers.detail: The channel below, which must deliver in order

viz.caption: THE ONE-OCTET HEADER AND THE NO-HEADER PACKET

cells: Inferred from in-order delivery and loss indication
Absent; context is verified periodically instead
The whole packet is the payload

viz.caption: THE THREE PACKET TYPES THIS PROFILE ADDS

items.label: CSP
items.desc: Context Synchronization Packet. Carries the compressed header but drops the payload, and includes the RTP payload length so the decompressor can infer the fields it needs.

items.label: CCP
items.desc: Context Check Packet. Carries only an optional 7-bit CRC, and is used to verify that the decompressor's context is still correct.

items.label: NHP
items.desc: No Header Packet. Consists only of the payload of the original packet, with the sequence number inferred by the assisting layer.

viz.caption: WHAT THE ASSISTING LAYER MUST TAKE OVER

items.title: Packet type identification
items.text: The assisting layer must tell the decompressor which packets have a header and which do not.

items.title: In-order delivery
items.text: The assisting layer must guarantee in-order delivery over the link, so the sequence number can be inferred.

items.title: Loss indication
items.text: The assisting layer must indicate every packet loss over the link.

items.title: No CRC needed
items.text: These three services together replace the checks that the CRC in the one-octet header used to do.

viz.caption: WHEN THE PROFILE PAYS OFF, AND WHEN IT CANNOT BE USED

items.title: Best case
items.text: Most packets become pure payload, with no header at all.

items.title: UDP checksum
items.text: The profile is not applicable if the 2-byte UDP checksum is enabled, which is always the case for IPv6/UDP.

items.title: IPv4
items.text: For IPv4/UDP the sender may choose to disable the UDP checksum.

items.title: Other traffic
items.text: For other applications, compression is carried out as with normal ROHC RTP.
